idiom_name: struct Effectivity { from: NaiveDate, until: Option<NaiveDate> } (chrono)
implementation_notes: The standard library has no calendar type: std::ops::Range<NaiveDate> is only a pair of bounds with a contains() method, it is not Copy because Range is an iterator, and there is no date arithmetic - so the period is your own two-field struct with Option<NaiveDate> for the open end, deriving Copy, Clone, Eq and PartialOrd to make the value semantics explicit. chrono supplies the civil date type (NaiveDate with from_ymd_opt, checked_add_days, ISO week and ordinal support and an independent Ord) and is the de-facto default. Keeping the range hand-written is also what lets the domain rule - non-empty period, non-overlap for one identity - live in the constructor.
pitfalls: Range<NaiveDate> looks like the obvious period type but is an iterator, not Copy, and carries no domain invariants: storing it means cloning on every use and leaves non-empty/non-overlap unchecked.

chrono, time and jiff each define their own date type; comparing NaiveDate with time::Date or jiff::civil::Date does not compile, and converting between them can shift the calendar assumption - pick one crate per project.

Option<NaiveDate> must be handled at every boundary: serialise the open end explicitly (null column or one documented sentinel) and reject until <= from in the constructor, or an empty period propagates silently.

variants.name: hand-written period over jiff::civil::Date
variants.implementation_notes: jiff separates civil time from absolute time by design - civil::Date is a calendar date with Ord/Eq and checked_add(Span) arithmetic, while Timestamp and Zoned cover instants - which is exactly the distinction a validity period needs; date differences come from Date::until/Date::since as a Span. Choose it for new code that will later need zone-aware arithmetic (jiff reads the system Time Zone Database and does DST-correct maths) and accept its recent MSRV; chrono remains the choice for existing code and the widest ecosystem.
variants.idiom_name: struct Effectivity { from: civil::Date, until: Option<civil::Date> } (jiff)
pitfalls: Ord gives comparisons, but arithmetic is explicit and fallible: adding a Span returns a Result, so "extend by one year" must handle the error instead of assuming success.
civil::Date is not an instant: turning it into a Timestamp needs a time zone, and reaching for Zoned just to compare two dates reintroduces the offset the civil type was meant to remove.
jiff's Span is not Eq in a field-wise sense (a comparison needs a relative date), so period length comparisons must go through Span::compare rather than ==
